claim: A sequence of comma-separated sentence-fragments can compress repeated effort across weeks or months into a single felt acceleration — the grammatical shorthand IS the time-compression. Billy renders weeks of ramp progress as 'Halfway there, two-thirds, three quarters.' — five words, three fragments, no full sentence. The reader doesn't need a sentence per week; the fragment-chain signals 'this happened many times, each time a little further,' and the missing grammar makes the pace feel like the progress itself. The expert layer is twofold: the items must be a measured PROGRESSION (each fragment advances on the last, so the chain has a vector, not just a list), and the move must STOP at the moment the progression completes, handing the reader straight into the scene that follows. This is the opposite of the common student instinct to narrate each iteration in full; the fragments do in five words what a paragraph of 'and then the next week' would do worse.

application.content: RHYTHM MOVE — sentence-fragment progression for time-compression. When you need to convey that something happened repeatedly, with incremental advance, over many units of time (weeks of practice, rising word-counts, growing distances, escalating attempts), do NOT narrate each iteration. Pick the measure that tracks the progress (a fraction, a count, a distance, a difficulty) and render three or four points on that scale as comma-separated FRAGMENTS — no full grammatical sentence: 'Halfway there, two-thirds, three quarters.' Requirements: (1) the fragments must ADVANCE — each one further along the same scale, so the chain has a direction; a list of unordered items is not this move. (2) Land the chain INTO the next beat — Billy goes straight from 'three quarters' to 'Until finally, I mustered up enough courage to complete my final challenge,' so the compression delivers the reader to the climax. (3) Keep it short (3-4 fragments); more and it stops compressing and starts cataloguing. Empirical anchor: Billy #07, 'Halfway there, two-thirds, three quarters.' (review: 'three sentence-fragments, comma-separated… the grammatical shorthand is doing time-compression work… the reader doesn't need full sentences for each iteration'). Authority: Tufte (Artful Sentences) devotes a chapter to short sentences and fragments as deliberate syntactic resources; Le Guin on rhythm as forward motion / pace. This is the EXPERT form of 'show progress' — not 'describe how you improved,' but compress the iteration into a beat.

workedExample.before: When I first started learning the violin I could barely play a single scale, but I practiced every single day, and over the first few months I slowly got better and was able to play simple songs, and then after about a year of consistent practice I could play more difficult pieces, and eventually, after nearly two years, I was finally able to perform a real concerto in front of an audience.
workedExample.after: The first year was scales. Then a folk tune I butchered nightly until I didn't. Then Bach, slow and wrong, then slow and right. Then the Bruch, the one I'd taped above my stand for two years, played whole, in front of a hall that went quiet.
workedExample.sourceRef: Composed to instantiate the VERIFIED fragment-progression time-compression move (Billy #07 'Halfway there, two-thirds, three quarters,' review 'Move 4'; Tufte on short sentences/fragments; Le Guin on pace). The BEFORE narrates each stage in full 'and then' clauses (flat, slow, telling); the AFTER compresses two years of practice into an advancing fragment-chain ('scales → folk tune → Bach slow-and-wrong then slow-and-right → the Bruch'), landing on the performance. NOT a quoted admit essay.
workedExample.usage: private-teaching-aid — DO NOT SURFACE and DO NOT MIMIC the violin scaffold or the exact fragment phrasing. It teaches the SYSTEM the compression mechanic; the generated chain must track the STUDENT'S own measure of progress.

application.mechanics: The lever is OMITTED grammar deployed as compression. (1) The fragments drop the repeated grammatical frame ('each week I reached…') that full sentences would force, so the eye and ear move fast — the speed of reading enacts the acceleration of progress. (2) The VECTOR: the fragments must be points on one measured scale, each advancing ('Halfway → two-thirds → three quarters'; 'scales → folk tune → Bach → the Bruch'), so the chain reads as a trajectory, not a heap. (3) The HANDOFF: the chain ends INTO the next beat (the climax, the scene, the turn) — it is a runway, not a destination. To transfer: identify the repeated activity and the single dimension along which it advanced; choose 3-4 milestone points on that dimension; render them as comma- or period-separated fragments with the repeated framing stripped; then write the sentence the chain was accelerating toward. Sub-lever: the fragments can be comma-spliced (Billy's 'Halfway there, two-thirds, three quarters') OR period-separated ('Scales. A folk tune. Bach.') — comma-splice compresses tighter and faster; periods give each milestone a beat of weight.
transfer: Language learning (rising counts): 'Ten words the first week. Forty. A hundred and twelve, counted on the bus home. Then the day I dreamed in Vietnamese and woke up arguing.' (Counts advance; lands on the milestone the chain was building to.)

Distance/endurance (comma-spliced, faster): 'Three blocks before I had to walk, then six, then the whole loop without stopping, then the loop twice before sunrise.' (Tighter comma-splice version; the missing grammar makes the months feel like one accelerating breath.)
failureModes: Fragments that don't advance — a list of unordered items ('the gym, the library, the lab, my room') is parataxis (003), not time-compression; this move REQUIRES a measured progression with a direction.
Too many fragments — six or eight milestones stop compressing and become a catalogue that drags more than the full sentences would; cap at 3-4.
No handoff — ending the essay or paragraph ON the fragment-chain with nothing after it leaves the compression pointing at nothing; the chain must deliver the reader into the next beat.
Using full grammatical sentences for each milestone — that is exactly the slow narration the move replaces; if each step is a complete sentence, you have not compressed anything.
application.antiTemplate: The MOVE (advancing fragment-chain that compresses repeated effort and lands into the next beat) transfers; the SHAPE must vary. Do NOT default to three fractions ('halfway, two-thirds, three quarters') — that is Billy's specific measure; the scale can be counts, distances, difficulty-of-repertoire, number of attempts, anything that advances. Vary comma-splice vs period-separated (different speeds and weights). Vary chain length within 3-4. Do NOT place the chain always at the same spot (Billy's is mid-essay before a climax; it could compress a long middle stretch the essay needs to get past quickly). And do NOT let the fragment-chain become a verbal mannerism the essay reaches for repeatedly — once is a craft move, twice is a tic.

sources.citation: Harvard 'Essays That Worked' corpus (Billy, 'Peabody Skatepark') + Uplift editorial review #07, 'Move 4 — sentence-fragment measurement sequence for incremental progress': 'Halfway there, two-thirds, three quarters.' is 'three sentence-fragments, comma-separated… No grammatical sentences; the sequence does the narrative work… the grammatical shorthand performs time-compression… the reader doesn't need full sentences for each iteration.'
sources.authorRole: Sponsored consultant feature (Crimson, admission unverified) + Uplift internal review — self-citation, Tier-2

sources.citation: Virginia Tufte, 'Artful Sentences: Syntax as Style' (Graphics Press) — organizes craft by syntactic concept, opening with a dedicated chapter on SHORT SENTENCES (and the deliberate use of fragments) as resources; thesis that 'syntax gives words the power to relate to each other in a sequence, to create rhythms and emphasis.' Grounds the fragment-chain as a recognized syntactic device for rhythm/emphasis rather than an error.
sources.authorRole: Named scholar of prose syntax; named-practitioner reference (Artful Sentences)

sources.citation: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'Steering the Craft,' ch. 'The Sound of Your Writing' — 'Pace and movement depend above all on rhythm'; the narrative sentence's duty is to 'lead to the next sentence.' Grounds the handoff requirement (the fragment-chain as a runway into the next beat).

connections.note: Fragment time-compression is an extreme, vectored parataxis (equal unranked items, but ADVANCING along one scale); 003 supplies the general parataxis principle, 004 the time-compression special case.
Both deploy omitted/minimal grammar for pacing; the beat-drop (002) is one short sentence on a pivot, the fragment-chain (004) is several advancing fragments that compress a stretch of time.

Compressing weeks into five words is restraint applied to TIME — trusting the reader to infer the iteration rather than narrating every instance, the same economy that names a thing once and orbits it.
